The purpose of this document is to replicate both synthetic experiments from @rue2023oracle.

```{r Packages}
library (dplyr)
```

```{r Refresh and Seed}
rm (list = ls())
set.seed (1234)
```

# Support Functions
Deterministic Multiplicative Incremental Quantile Estimator (DUMIQE), based on @DUMIQE_algorithm. This article provides a more detailed explanation of the initialization step of the DUMIQE algorithm. In the experiments presented in @rue2023oracle, there is no need to account for negative quantiles or the possibility of the algorithm producing quantile estimates equal to zero. Therefore, this document presents a simplified version of the DUMIQE algorithm.
```{r DUMIQE Algorithm}
D1 <- function (q_prob, q_hat) {
    return(q_prob * q_hat)
}
D2 <- function (q_prob, q_hat) {
    return((1 - q_prob) * q_hat)
}

# Incremental Algorithm (returns next iteration quantile estimates for each lambda_vec value)
DUMIQE <- function (t, x_obs, q_hat_t, lambda_vec, q_prob) {
    if (t == 0) { # Initialization step 
    Q_min <- 14 # I'm choosing a different value until it converges...
    return (rep (Q_min, times = length(lambda_vec))) # L was still not defined
    } else {
        return(ifelse (
            x_obs[t + 1] >= q_hat_t,                    # Logical vector
            # RECALL: between 2 vectors * performs element-wise multiplication 
            q_hat_t + lambda_vec * D1(q_prob, q_hat_t), # If TRUE
            q_hat_t - lambda_vec * D2(q_prob, q_hat_t)  # If FALSE
        )) 
    }
}
```

Quantile Loss function on iteration t 
```{r QL function}
QL <- function (t, x_obs, q_hat_t, q_prob) {
    return(ifelse(
        x_obs[t + 1] >= q_hat_t,               # Logical vector
        (1-q_prob) * (x_obs[t + 1] - q_hat_t), # If TRUE
        q_prob * (q_hat_t - x_obs[t + 1])      # If FALSE
    ))
}
```

# Figure 2
Replicating Figure 2 (synthetic) experiment.

## Data stream generation 
Change-point at time t = T. The number of observations in each data stream is $2\text{T}$.
```{r Simulate Data} 
tau1  <- 500
tau2  <- 10^4
T     <- 10^4
tau_n <- function (t) {
    return(tau1 * as.integer(t < T) + tau2 * as.integer(t >= T & t < 2*T))
}
iter <- 0:(2*T - 1)

# Normally distributed data stream
miu    <- 8
b      <- 2
sigma  <- 1
t      <- iter
mean_t <- miu + b * sin(2 * pi * t / tau_n(t))
normal_stream <- rnorm(
    n = 2*T,
    mean = mean_t,
    sd = sigma
)
```

```{r Real Quantiles (to track)}
q_fig2 <- 0.7
```

## \textit{Oracle} Approach
```{r Tuning Parameters}
possible_lambdas <- exp(seq (from = -7, to = 0, by = 0.05))
L <- length(possible_lambdas) # number of estimates per iteration 

gamma_Oracle <- 1 - (0.01)^(1/1000) # 0.005 
```

```{r Oracle Algorithm}
q_hat   <- matrix(0, nrow = 2*T, ncol = L)
QL_hat  <- matrix(0, nrow = 2*T, ncol = L)
EQL_hat <- matrix(0, nrow = 2*T, ncol = L)

oracle_lambdas         <- numeric(2*T)
oracle_quantiles       <- numeric(2*T)
oracle_QL              <- numeric(2*T)

for (t in iter) {
    # Quantiles estimates on iteration t for each value in possible_lambdas 
    q_hat[t + 1, ] <- DUMIQE(
        t, 
        normal_stream, 
        q_hat[max(t,1), ], # max is due to the initialization step
        possible_lambdas,
        q_fig2
    )

    QL_hat[t + 1, ] <- QL(t, normal_stream, q_hat[t + 1, ], q_fig2)

    # Expected Quantile Loss (EQL) function on iteration t. It is based on the exponentially weighted moving average.
    # It was previously defined as a function, but the node stack overflow error was thrown given it was defined recursively (so, e.g., it was evaluating all the previous steps creating very deep stack call)
    if (t == 0) {
        EQL_hat[t + 1, ] <- QL_hat[t + 1, ] # Initialization
    } else {
        EQL_hat[t + 1, ] <-
            (1 - gamma_Oracle) * EQL_hat[t, ] +
            gamma_Oracle * QL_hat[t + 1, ]
    }

    index <- which.min(EQL_hat[t + 1, ])
    # The Oracle approach stores the lambda value with the minimum estimated EQL
    oracle_lambdas [t + 1]  <- possible_lambdas[index]
    oracle_quantiles[t + 1] <- q_hat[t + 1, index]
    oracle_QL [t + 1]       <- QL_hat[t + 1, index]
}
```

## Diagnostics Plots
Tracking the q = 0.7 quantile using the Oracle approach. 

In the upper left panel, we see that quantile loss quickly decreases and then stabilizes. The initial value of the quantile tracking algorithm is outside the data stream distribution. Therefore, in the initial phase, the quantile loss is high and a high value of $\lambda$ (update size) is used for the tracking algorithm to quickly get within the data stream distribution. When the quantile tracking algorithm is within the data stream distribution, a smaller $\lambda$ is optimal and the value of $\lambda$ is reduced. The expected quantile loss is reduced accordingly. 

Estimated QL in every iteration. 
```{r Estimated QL by iteration graph}
plot(
    x = iter,
    y = oracle_QL,
    type = "l", # Line Plot
    ylim = c(0,1),
    xlab = "Iteration",
    ylab = "QL"
)
```

Resulting recursive updating of $\lambda$. The symbol $\lambda_{\text{opt}}$ refers to the value resulting in the minimal estimated QL. The gray lines refer to theoretically optimal values of $\lambda$.

The black lines in the top right panel show the optimal value of $\lambda$ for the data stream dynamics before and after the concept change at iteration 10 000. We see that a larger step size is needed to efficiently track rapid variations. We further see that the Oracle approach uses step lengths close to the optimal step lengths.

```{r Recursive Lambda Updating graph}
    x = iter,
    y = theoretical_lambdas,
    col = "grey", # Light Grey (or Gray?)
    lty = 1 # Should be the same line type as the other (only the colour should change)

    "topright",

```

Resulting tracking. The gray dots represent the normal data stream in and the black line is tracking.
```{r Quantile Tracking Plot}
plot(
    x = iter,
    y = oracle_quantiles, # Estimated Quantiles...
    type = "p", # Points Plot
    pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
    col = "red",  
    ylim = c(0,14),
    xlab = "Iteration",
    ylab = expression("Quantile at " ~ q == 0.7)
)

lines(
    x = iter,
    y = normal_stream,
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
)
```
